column2: This world is mere change, and this life, opinion.
Look within; within is the fountain of all good.
Begin therefore with little things.
Exercise, therefore, what is in your power.
Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.
Nothing can bring you peace but yourself.
Simplify, simplify.
Only that day dawns to which we are awake.
Eat not to dullness; drink not to elevation.
Resolve to perform what you ought; perform without fail what you resolve.
From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom.
I finally succeeded in learning to read.
I let no opportunity slip to push my case.
Cast down your bucket where you are.
He worked patiently for success; and it came, but slowly.
Progress, however, of the best kind, is comparatively slow.
The spectacle of effort is what awakens and sustains our own effort.
To face uninteresting drudgery is a good part of life's work.
Dreams are the seedlings of realities.
Self-control is strength; Right Thought is mastery; Calmness is power.
Let these things suffice thee; let them be always unto thee, as thy general rules and precepts.
Give thyself leisure to learn some good thing, and cease roving and wandering to and fro.
Our life is a warfare, and a mere pilgrimage.
Trouble not thyself any more henceforth, reduce thyself unto perfect simplicity.
Doth any man offend? It is against himself that he doth offend: why should it trouble thee?
Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of things.
Upon every accident, remember to turn toward yourself and inquire what faculty you have for its use.
Never say of anything, “I have lost it,” but, “I have restored it.”
For this is your business—to act well the given part, but to choose it belongs to another.
For if you once gain time and respite, you will more easily command yourself.
Whoso would be a man, must be a nonconformist.
Nothing is at last sacred but the integrity of your own mind.
A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds, adored by little statesmen and philosophers and divines.
Insist on yourself; never imitate.
Our strength grows out of our weakness.
The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.
In the long run men hit only what they aim at.
Every path but your own is the path of fate.
The universe is wider than our views of it.
Things do not change; we change.
Speak not but what may benefit others or yourself; avoid trifling conversation.
Let all your things have their places; let each part of your business have its time.
Lose no time; be always employ'd in something useful; cut off all unnecessary actions.
Wrong none by doing injuries, or omitting the benefits that are your duty.
Be not disturbed at trifles, or at accidents common or unavoidable.
A man is literally what he thinks, his character being the complete sum of all his thoughts.

column2: The silver trump of freedom had roused my soul to eternal wakefulness.
Freedom now appeared, to disappear no more forever.
You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.
It recalled the departed self-confidence, and inspired me again with a determination to be free.
It was a glorious resurrection, from the tomb of slavery, to the heaven of freedom.
I have found that the happiest people are those who do the most for others.
But I was determined to succeed.
I learned that assistance given to the weak makes the one who gives it strong.
I have always had more of an ambition to do things than merely to talk about doing them.
It is at the bottom of life we must begin, and not at the top.
The spirit of self-help is the root of all genuine growth in the individual.
Help from without is often enfeebling in its effects, but help from within invariably invigorates.
National progress is the sum of individual industry, energy, and uprightness.
Fortune has often been blamed for her blindness; but fortune is not so blind as men are.
It is not ease, but effort—not facility, but difficulty, that makes men.
Education is for behavior, and habits are the stuff of which behavior consists.

column2: Adults ages 18–60 generally need at least seven hours of sleep each day.
Adults ages 61–64 generally need seven to nine hours of sleep.
Adults 65 and older generally need seven to eight hours of sleep.
Healthy sleep depends on quality as well as total time asleep.
Enough sleep supports mood, attention, memory, heart health, and metabolism.
A consistent bedtime and wake time can support better sleep.
A quiet, relaxing, cool bedroom is more sleep-friendly.
Turning electronics off at least 30 minutes before bed may help sleep.
Large meals and alcohol close to bedtime can interfere with sleep.
Afternoon or evening caffeine can make sleep harder.
Children ages 3–5 should be active throughout the day; caregivers can aim for three hours.
Youth ages 6–17 need at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily.
Adults gain substantial benefits from 150–300 weekly minutes of moderate aerobic activity.
Adults also benefit from muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days each week.
For adults, moving more and sitting less is a core health guideline.
More sedentary time is associated with higher heart-disease, blood-pressure, and mortality risk.
Even small amounts of moderate-to-vigorous activity provide some benefit.
Physical activity no longer needs to occur in ten-minute blocks to count.
One session of activity can reduce short-term anxiety.
Immediate activity benefits can include lower blood pressure and better insulin sensitivity.
Regular activity is linked with lower risks of heart disease, stroke, diabetes, depression, and dementia.
For older adults, regular activity lowers the risk of falls and fall injuries.
Healthy diets are built around adequacy, balance, moderation, and diversity.
Minimally processed foods low in excess sodium, sugars, and unhealthy fats form a sound foundation.
For most people, unrefined carbohydrates can supply about 45–75% of daily energy.
Whole grains, vegetables, fruits, and pulses are preferred carbohydrate sources.
People older than ten should aim for at least 400 grams of fruit and vegetables daily.
People older than ten should aim for at least 25 grams of naturally occurring fibre daily.
Free sugars should stay below 10% of daily energy; 5% or less may add benefit.
WHO advises reducing free sugar without relying on non-sugar sweeteners.
For adults, keeping total fat near or below 30% of energy may help prevent unhealthy weight gain.
Unsaturated fats are preferable to saturated and trans fats.
Saturated fat should stay below 10% of energy and trans fat below 1%.
Adults should limit salt below five grams daily, equivalent to two grams of sodium.
Getting enough water helps prevent dehydration and supports normal body function.
Dehydration can make thinking less clear.
Dehydration can affect mood.
Water helps the body regulate temperature.
Dehydration can contribute to constipation and kidney stones.
Replacing sugary drinks with plain water can reduce calorie intake.
Water needs vary with age, sex, pregnancy, breastfeeding, activity, and environment.
Water-rich foods such as fruits and vegetables contribute to daily fluid intake.
The relaxation response is associated with slower breathing and a lower heart rate.
Relaxation can also lower blood pressure and reduce oxygen use.
Progressive relaxation alternates deliberate muscle tension with release.
Guided imagery uses calming imagined scenes or events to evoke relaxation.
Relaxation exercises should complement—not replace—appropriate medical care.
Mindfulness trains attention toward the present moment without judgment.
Large reviews find mindfulness can outperform no treatment for anxiety and depression.
Mindfulness may improve sleep, but does not necessarily outperform CBT or exercise.
Meditation evidence is varied, and benefits are sometimes interpreted too optimistically.
A 2020 review found negative meditation experiences in about 8% of participants.
Social connection includes relationship structure, exchanged support, and interaction quality.
Social isolation is objective; loneliness is the subjective feeling of insufficient connection.
WHO estimates that roughly one in six people worldwide experiences loneliness.
Adolescents report loneliness more often than many older age groups.
WHO estimates loneliness is more common in low-income countries than high-income countries.
Health, income, life changes, living arrangements, community resources, and digital use can affect connection.
Social disconnection is associated with physical and mental health risks.
Students who feel connected tend to perform better at school.
Communities with strong social ties tend to be safer and more resilient.
Reaching out, listening fully, joining a group, or volunteering are practical ways to build connection.
One field study repeated a chosen health behavior in the same context for 12 weeks.
Habit automaticity rose quickly at first and then approached a plateau.
Time to near-maximum automaticity varied widely—from 18 to 254 days.
The habit study's median was 66 days, not the popular 21-day rule.
Missing one opportunity did not materially derail habit formation in that study.
Practice tests can strengthen long-term memory, not merely measure it.
Repeated study produced better recall after five minutes in two experiments.
After two days or one week, prior testing beat repeated study despite lower learner confidence.
Durable learning usually benefits from revisiting material on multiple occasions.
The most useful gap between study sessions grows as the desired retention period grows.
Although the useful study gap grew, it represented a smaller share of longer retention intervals.
Light is the strongest environmental cue for synchronizing the human circadian system.
Light entering the eyes informs the brain's master clock about day and night.
Morning light can promote wakefulness and alertness.
More evening light can delay sleep timing.
Gradually shifting sleep, meals, activity, and light can make clock changes easier to adapt to.
Urban green spaces can encourage activity while supporting relaxation and stress relief.
Green spaces may support health through social cohesion and reduced heat, noise, and air pollution.
Teenagers ages 13–17 generally need eight to ten hours of sleep.
Children ages 6–12 generally need nine to twelve hours of sleep.
Children ages 3–5 generally need ten to thirteen hours of sleep, including naps.
Toddlers ages 1–2 generally need eleven to fourteen hours of sleep, including naps.
Infants ages 4–12 months generally need twelve to sixteen hours of sleep, including naps.
Repeated waking can be a sign of poor sleep quality even when total sleep time seems adequate.
A sleep diary can help reveal patterns in bedtime, waking, naps, exercise, and caffeine use.
Physical activity can improve sleep quality as well as reduce anxiety.
Older adults benefit from a mix of aerobic, muscle-strengthening, and balance activities.
Pregnant and postpartum adults can usually aim for 150 weekly minutes of moderate aerobic activity.
Activity can improve cognition for young people ages 6–13.
People with chronic conditions or disabilities can still gain important benefits from suitable activity.
Green-space benefits can arise through exercise, relaxation, social contact, and reduced environmental exposure.
Accessible green spaces can support both physical and mental health across population groups.
Urban green spaces can give neighbors places to meet, strengthening social cohesion.
